back: A normal host process started with namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (how much it can use). No guest kernel.

front: Container vs VM: the core trade?
back: Containers share the host kernel: near-zero overhead and fast start, but weaker isolation. VMs have their own kernel behind a hypervisor.
PID, network, mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, user, cgroup. Each gives the process a private copy of one global resource.

front: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
back: The kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL. Exit code 137 (128 + 9), reason OOMKilled, no stack trace.

front: How is a CPU limit enforced?
back: As a CFS quota per period (default 100 ms). 2 CPUs = 200 ms per 100 ms; once used, all threads pause until the next period.
Tail latency spikes while average CPU looks fine. Check the cgroup throttled-period counters.

front: Why did old JVMs get OOM-killed in containers?
back: They sized the default heap from host RAM (1/4 of 64 GB = 16 GB) and ignored the cgroup limit. Fixed in JDK 10 and 8u191.

front: What is an image made of?
back: An ordered list of read-only, content-addressed layer tarballs plus a manifest and config (command, env, user, ports), per the OCI image spec.

front: How does a container write to a file from a lower layer?
back: Copy-on-write: overlayfs copies the file up into the container's thin writable layer, then modifies it there.
A tag (:1.4, :latest) is a movable pointer. A digest (sha256:...) is the hash of the manifest and names exact bytes. Deploy by digest.

front: Does deleting a file in a later layer shrink the image?
back: No. The earlier layer still holds it; the later layer only adds a whiteout. Secrets leak this way.
Least-changing first: base, then dependency manifest and install, then source. A change invalidates its layer and every layer after it.
Compile in a build stage with all the tools, then COPY --from=build only the output into a small final image.
nodes × image size ÷ registry bandwidth. 200 × 1.1 GB ÷ 1.25 GB/s ≈ 176 s before new capacity serves.

front: Docker's stack from CLI to kernel?
back: docker CLI → dockerd → containerd → runc, which sets up namespaces and cgroups and starts the process.
Sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period (10 s by default), then SIGKILL.
Shell form makes /bin/sh PID 1, which does not forward SIGTERM, so the app never drains and is SIGKILLed.
Injected at run time (env vars, mounted files, secrets store). Build one image and promote the same digest everywhere.
